messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 49

**Patient Vignette: Arjun (Age 29, Painter)**

Arjun is a 29-year-old South Asian man, married for three years, who works as a painter for a residential renovation company. He presents with a guarded, soft-spoken demeanor, his hands often resting still in his lap, the calluses and faint paint stains on his fingers the only visible trace of his work.

The event that changed everything happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late November. Arjun had just finished a job at a client’s house in a neighborhood he did not know well. He was walking the three blocks to the bus stop, his canvas tool bag slung over one shoulder, his phone in his hand to check the schedule. He remembers the street was quiet, the air cold and damp. He heard footsteps behind him, but it was a city street; he did not turn around. Then, a hand grabbed his collar, yanking him backward. He remembers a flash of a dark jacket, a voice—low, flat, not shouting—telling him to give it up. He froze. He handed over his phone. Then the man demanded his wallet. Arjun fumbled, his hands shaking, and pulled it from his back pocket. The man grabbed it, and then, without warning, struck Arjun across the side of the head with something hard—Arjun thinks it was the butt of a small gun, but he never saw it clearly. He went down to his knees on the cold asphalt, the impact a bright, silent explosion in his right ear. The man ran. Arjun knelt there for a long time, his tool bag still on his shoulder, his head throbbing, the sound of his own breath loud in the sudden silence.

In the weeks that followed, Arjun did not tell his wife, Priya, the full story. He said he was mugged, that it was over quickly, that he was fine. But he was not fine. He stopped taking the bus. He began driving their old car to every job site, even if it meant sitting in traffic for an hour. He started checking the locks on their apartment door three times before bed. At work, he found himself unable to focus on the clean lines of a trim or the smooth finish of a wall. His hand would tremble when holding a brush, and he would see, in the corner of his eye, a shadow that was not there. He began to avoid certain neighborhoods, even if it meant losing a contract. His foreman noticed he was slower, more withdrawn, and would sometimes just stand in the middle of a room, staring at a blank wall, his brush dripping paint onto the drop cloth.

The nightmares started about a month later. They are not a replay of the event. They are worse. In the dreams, he is painting a ceiling, and the ceiling begins to crumble, raining down cold, black water. Or he is walking down a long, empty hallway, and the floor turns to gravel. He wakes up with his heart pounding, convinced he is about to be hit again. He has not slept through the night in six months.

Priya has become worried. She tells him he is not the same man she married. He is irritable, easily startled. If she comes up behind him in the kitchen, he flinches and snaps at her. He has stopped going to temple with her on Sundays, saying he is too tired. He has stopped painting at home, his easel collecting dust in the corner of the living room. He used to find a quiet peace in mixing colors, in the slow, deliberate act of creating something. Now, the smell of turpentine makes his stomach clench. It reminds him of the cold, damp air of that street.

He sits in the session with his hands clasped tightly. He does not make eye contact for long. When asked about the mugging, he gives a short, factual account, then falls silent. He says he does not think about it. But he also admits he has not walked alone after dark in eight months. He says he is fine, that it was just a random thing, that he should be over it by now. But his body tells a different story: the way his shoulders are perpetually hunched, the way his eyes dart to the door when he hears a noise in the hallway, the way he flinches when a car backfires outside the window. He is a man living in a world that has become menacing, a world where a quiet street can turn into a trap, where a hand on his collar is not a greeting but a threat. He is still painting, but the colors have all gone gray.
